topics.topic: Development of practical skills in physics

questions.prompt:
A ray enters a polymer block at 40° and refracts at 22°, each angle measured to ±2°.
(i) Calculate the refractive index. (2)
(ii) Use maximum and minimum angles to estimate the absolute uncertainty in n. (3)
Describe how to reduce the uncertainty in a refractive index measurement using a glass block and ray box. (4)
questions.solution:
Use a narrow beam and mark rays with crosses far apart [B1]
Measure r for a wide range of i [B1]
Plot sin i against sin r [B1]
Gradient = n; worst-fit line gives uncertainty [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain the advantage of timing 10 oscillations. (2)
(ii) A graph of T² against L has gradient 4.0 s² m⁻¹. Calculate g. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Same reaction-time uncertainty over a longer time [B1]
Smaller percentage uncertainty in T [B1]
(ii) g = 4π² ÷ 4.0 [M1]
= 9.9 m s⁻² [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why shorter pendulums have a greater percentage uncertainty in period. (2)
questions.solution:
Period is smaller [B1]
Same timing uncertainty is a larger percentage [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to determine the conductivity of a metal wire. (4)
questions.solution:
Measure diameter at several places with a micrometer; calculate A [B1]
Measure V and I for several lengths L [B1]
Calculate conductance G = I/V [B1]
Plot G against 1/L; gradient = σA [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A micrometer has 50 divisions per 0.5 mm rotation. State its resolution. (1)
(ii) A wire has diameter (0.35 ± 0.02) mm. Calculate its area and absolute uncertainty. (2)
Explain how to tell whether light reflected from a glass block is polarised using one polarising filter. (3)
questions.solution:
View the reflected light through the filter [B1]
Rotate the filter through 360° [B1]
If the intensity varies (with minima), the light is polarised [B1]

questions.prompt: A gauge reads 250 kPa above atmospheric (100 kPa). State the absolute pressure with its unit. (2)

A lemon cell gives 738 mV across 10.0 kΩ and 765 mV across 13.3 kΩ.
(i) Calculate each current. (1)
(ii) Use the two points to find the internal resistance. (2)

(i) Use 738 mV at 73.8 μA and r = 1.66 kΩ to find the lemon's e.m.f. (1)
(ii) Explain why two lemons in series can't light a 1.5 V, 0.45 W lamp. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) ε = 0.738 + 73.8 × 10⁻⁶ × 1660 = 0.86 V [B1]
(ii) Lamp needs 0.30 A [M1]
Maximum current ≈ 1.72 ÷ 3320 = 0.5 mA – far too small [A1]

questions.prompt: Two identical cells (ε, r) in parallel supply total current I. Derive the e.m.f. equation. (2)
questions.solution:
Each cell carries I/2 [M1]
ε = V + Ir/2 [A1]

questions.prompt:
An LED's striking voltage readings are 1.42, 1.48, 1.50 and 1.55 V.
(i) Calculate the mean and absolute uncertainty. (2)
(ii) Describe one major cause of uncertainty and how to reduce it. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Mean = 1.49 V [B1]
± 0.07 V [B1]
(ii) Hard to judge when the LED first glows [B1]
View through a dark tube / use a light sensor [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Show that h = gradient × e/c for a graph of striking voltage against 1/λ. (2)
(ii) The gradient is 8.90 × 10⁻⁷ V m. Calculate h. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) eV = hc/λ, so V = (hc/e)(1/λ) [M1]
Gradient = hc/e, so h = gradient × e/c [A1]
(ii) h = 8.90 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 3.00 × 10⁸ [M1]
= 4.7 × 10⁻³⁴ J s [A1]

questions.prompt:
A capacitor's p.d. is 7.00 V at 0 s and 0.94 V at 50 s, readings every 10 s.
(i) Describe a test for exponential decay. (2)
(ii) Show the time constant is about 25 s. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Calculate the ratio of successive readings at equal time intervals [B1]
Constant ratio means exponential [B1]
(ii) Gradient of ln V against t = (ln 0.94 − ln 7.00) ÷ 50 = −0.040 s⁻¹ [M1]
τ = 1 ÷ 0.040 = 25 s [A1]

questions.prompt: A capacitor discharging through 4.7 kΩ has τ = 25 s. Calculate C. (1)

(i) Show that after 5τ the stored energy is 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ of its initial value. (3)
(ii) Explain why engineers treat 5τ as fully discharged. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) V = V₀e⁻⁵ [M1]
E ∝ V², so E = E₀e⁻¹⁰ [M1]
= 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ E₀ [A1]
(ii) Remaining energy is negligible, so it's safe to handle [B1]

questions.prompt:
A nichrome wire of diameter 0.52 ± 0.01 mm carries 0.29 ± 0.01 A. The gradient of V against L is 1.40 V m⁻¹.
(i) Calculate the resistivity. (2)
(ii) Calculate its percentage uncertainty. (2)
Explain how a graph of V against L changes if the current isn't kept constant. (3)
questions.solution:
Longer wire means higher resistance [B1]
Current decreases [B1]
So V rises less than proportionally: graph curves [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to measure the Young modulus of a metal wire. (4)
questions.solution:
Measure length with a metre rule and diameter with a micrometer at several points [B1]
Add masses and measure extension with a vernier scale/marker [B1]
Plot stress against strain [B1]
E = gradient of the linear region [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what corrected count rate means and how it's found. (2)
questions.solution:
Measure background count rate without the source [B1]
Subtract it from each measured count rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a fixed resistor is in series with a diode when plotting its I–V graph. (2)
questions.solution:
Limits the current once the diode conducts [B1]
Protects the diode from damage [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to measure fringe separation accurately. (2)
questions.solution:
Measure across many fringes with a ruler/travelling microscope [B1]
Divide by the number of spacings [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the output voltmeter is across the fixed resistor rather than the thermistor. (1)
questions.solution: Output rises as temperature rises (thermistor resistance falls) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a graph of height against t² gives g. (2)

A length is measured as (2.40 ± 0.05) m.
(a) Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2)
(b) The length is squared to obtain an area proportional to $L^2$. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the area. (2)
(c) Explain the difference between a random and a systematic error. (3)
hints: For powers, multiply fractional uncertainty by the power.
questions.solution:
(a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.05/2.40\times100=2.08\%$. [M1 A1]
(b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. [M1 A1]
(c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [B1 B1 B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Calculate the number of bits needed for 4096 grey levels. (1)
(ii) Calculate the memory in bytes for an uncompressed 2000 × 1500 pixel image with 4096 grey levels. (3)
Explain why a log-log graph is used to compare detector responses over a wide intensity range. (2)
questions.solution:
Data span several orders of magnitude [B1]
Power-law relationships appear as straight lines [B1]

questions.prompt: State the minimum sampling rate for sound up to 20 kHz and why. (2)
questions.solution:
40 kHz [B1]
Must sample at least twice the highest frequency [B1]

questions.prompt: A camera has 12 million pixels each with 24 bits. Calculate the information per image in MB. (2)
V is measured to ±2% and I to ±3%. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in R = V/I. (2)
Calculate the voltage resolution of an 8-bit ADC with a 5.12 V range. (2)
A signal varies over 5.0 V with noise of 0.1 V. Calculate the number of useful bits. (2)
State the unit siemens in terms of the ohm. (1)

(i) Calculate the time to download a 1.5 GB file at 30 Mbit s⁻¹. (2)
(ii) A soundtrack is sampled at 16.0 kHz. State and explain the highest frequency it can record. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 1.5 × 10⁹ × 8 ÷ 3.0 × 10⁷ [M1]
= 400 s [A1]
(ii) 8.0 kHz [B1]
Sampling must be at least twice the signal frequency [B1]

questions.prompt: An LDR is in series with a 400 kΩ resistor across 6.00 V. The highest LDR p.d. is (3.00 ± 0.01) V. Calculate the LDR resistance and its uncertainty. (2)
questions.solution:
R = 400 kΩ [B1]
± 3 kΩ (from 3.01 V and 2.99 V) [B1]

questions.prompt: Show that E/c has units of momentum. (1)
questions.solution: kg m² s⁻² ÷ m s⁻¹ = kg m s⁻¹ [B1]

questions.prompt: Wire diameters are 0.32, 0.33, 0.33, 0.34 and 0.39 mm. Identify the outlier, then find the mean and its percentage uncertainty. (3)
questions.solution:
0.39 mm is an outlier [B1]
Mean = 0.33 ± 0.01 mm [B1]
≈ 3% [B1]

questions.prompt: Mass is 25.6 ± 0.2 g and volume 5.2 ± 0.4 cm³. Calculate the density and its uncertainty. (2)

A webcam captures 1280 × 720 pixels at 24 bits per pixel.
(i) Calculate the bits in one image. (1)
(ii) A 40-minute recording at 30 images per second is 0.74 GB. Show the average image is about 82 kbit. (2)
(iii) Calculate the compression factor. (1)
A 2.56 mV signal has noise of 2.5 × 10⁻³ mV and a maximum frequency of 8000 Hz. Find the number of bits needed and the minimum sampling rate. (2)
Explain why a rapidly varying signal can't be reconstructed accurately at the same sampling rate. (2)
questions.solution:
Signal changes between samples, so detail is lost [B1]
Sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency [B1]

questions.prompt: A trace has 4 divisions per cycle at 50 ms/div and a peak of 3 divisions at 0.2 V/div. Find the frequency and amplitude. (2)
Express N m⁻¹ in base units. (1)
Express the farad in base units. (2)
questions.solution:
F = A s ÷ V [M1]
= A² s⁴ kg⁻¹ m⁻² [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a logarithmic axis is used for wavelength on an atmospheric transmission graph, and one drawback. (2)
questions.solution:
Covers many orders of magnitude [B1]
Hard to read intermediate values / judge widths [B1]

questions.prompt: Estimate the ratio of nuclear diameter to atomic diameter. (1)
Gas volume is 47 ± 1 cm³ at 30 ± 1 °C. Find the percentage uncertainties in V and in absolute temperature. (2)
A 5.0 V signal with 4.9 mV noise is sampled at 12 kHz. Find the useful bits per sample and the highest frequency recorded. (2)
questions.solution:
About 1000 levels: 10 bits [B1]
Highest frequency 6 kHz [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the information in a 1900 × 1100 pixel image with 3 bytes per pixel. (1)
Temperature rises from 53.4 ± 0.2 °C to 96.1 ± 0.2 °C in 10 s. Give the rate and uncertainty. (1)
How many bits are needed for 1 185 856 000 alternatives? (1)
Calculate the data in an 1136 × 640 pixel image at 3 bytes per pixel. (1)

(i) Show CD audio (44 kHz, 16-bit, stereo) exceeds 1 Mbit s⁻¹. (1)
(ii) Show 840 MB plays for about 80 minutes. (2)
A 2 mV signal has 75 μV noise. Find the bits needed. (2)

(i) An echo returns after 15.5 μs in tissue (1540 m s⁻¹). Calculate the depth. (1)
(ii) A 1 μs pulse is used. Estimate the longitudinal resolution. (2)
A diode passes 7.5 ± 0.02 mA at 0.65 ± 0.02 V. Calculate its conductance and uncertainty. (2)
Wire diameter readings give 0.250 mm ± 0.003 mm. Calculate the area and its percentage uncertainty. (2)
A 4.0 m wire of diameter 0.50 mm has a force-extension gradient of 1.0 × 10⁴ N m⁻¹. Calculate its Young modulus. (3)
Explain the shape of the force-extension graph of a rubber band in terms of its molecular structure. (4)
questions.solution:
Long tangled polymer chains [B1]
Initially chains straighten easily – low stiffness [B1]
Once straight, bonds stretch – stiffer [B1]
Unloading curve lies below loading (hysteresis) – energy dissipated [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the stress-strain graph for a ductile metal beyond the elastic limit. (2)
questions.solution:
Large plastic strain for small increase in stress [B1]
Necking before fracture [B1]

questions.prompt: A 2.0 m wire of area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² extends 1.0 mm under 100 N. Calculate its Young modulus. (2)
Give two precautions when loading a wire or rubber band to breaking. (2)
questions.solution:
Wear eye protection [B1]
Use a sand tray / keep feet clear of masses [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the stress-strain behaviour of a rubber polymer. (2)
questions.solution:
Very large elastic strain [B1]
Non-linear with hysteresis [B1]

questions.prompt:
A 1.4 m wire (A = 0.52 × 10⁻⁶ m², E = 2.8 × 10¹¹ Pa) has yield stress 3.5 × 10⁸ Pa.
(i) Calculate its extension at yield. (2)
(ii) Calculate the energy stored at yield. (2)

(i) The wire's length is doubled. State the effect on yield strain and energy stored at yield. (2)
(ii) Explain why long cables tow oil rigs. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Yield strain unchanged [B1]
Energy stored doubles [B1]
(ii) Long cable stores more energy before yielding [B1]
Absorbs sudden jerks without breaking [B1]

questions.prompt: A 240 m rope of diameter 12.0 mm (E = 13.2 GPa) carries 550 N. Calculate its extension. (2)

(i) A wire extends 0.50 mm under 10 N. Calculate its stiffness. (2)
(ii) Calculate the oscillation period with the 10 N load. (2)
Explain the stress-strain behaviour of a metal alloy and of rubber in terms of microstructure. (4)
questions.solution:
Alloy: atoms bonded in a lattice; small strain is bond stretching (linear) [B1]
Impurity atoms pin dislocations, raising the yield point [B1]
Rubber: tangled polymer chains straighten at low stress [B1]
Once straight, bonds stretch, so it stiffens [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a loaded wire oscillates with SHM but a rubber strip doesn't. (2)
questions.solution:
Wire obeys Hooke's law: restoring force ∝ displacement [B1]
Rubber's force-extension graph isn't linear [B1]

questions.prompt: State one property each of ceramics and ductile metals. (2)
questions.solution:
Ceramics are brittle / stiff [B1]
Ductile metals can be drawn into wires [B1]

questions.prompt: Under the same force and length: X has area A and extension x, Y has 2A and x/4, Z has A/2 and 4x. Order their Young moduli. (2)
questions.solution:
E_X = k, E_Y = 2k, E_Z = k/2 [M1]
Y > X > Z [A1]

questions.prompt: State two main sources of uncertainty in measuring a wire's Young modulus. (2)
questions.solution:
Diameter: small, squared in area [B1]
Extension: small and hard to measure [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A filament bulb has 4 V across it in series with 3.4 Ω on 12 V. Show R ≈ 2 Ω. (2)
(ii) Its filament is 0.046 mm in diameter and 20 cm long. Calculate the conductivity. (2)
Spider silk has strength 1.4 GPa and density 1.2 × 10³ kg m⁻³; steel 2.8 GPa and 7.8 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Show silk's strength-to-weight is about 3 times steel's. (2)
A copper wire (area 5.90 × 10⁻⁸ m²) stretches from 3.951 m to 3.953 m under 3.43 N. Calculate E. (2)

Gold has density 19 320 kg m⁻³ and molar mass 0.197 kg mol⁻¹.
(i) Show there are about 6 × 10²⁸ atoms m⁻³. (2)
(ii) With 74% packing, calculate the atomic radius. (2)
Silver has density 10 500 kg m⁻³ and atomic mass 1.8 × 10⁻²⁵ kg. Estimate an atom's diameter. (2)

A 0.059 kg ball hangs on a cord: natural length 1.15 m, 1.31 m at rest, 1.78 m at its lowest.
(i) Show k ≈ 3.7 N m⁻¹. (1)
(ii) Calculate the energy stored at rest. (1)
(iii) Calculate the maximum upward acceleration. (2)

Two resistors, 100 $\Omega$ and 200 $\Omega$, are connected in series to an ideal 6 V supply.
(a) Calculate the current. (2)
(b) Calculate the potential difference across the 200 $\Omega$ resistor. (2)
(c) Explain how the total current would change if the resistors were connected in parallel instead. (2)
questions.solution:
(a) $R_T=300\,\Omega$, so $I=V/R=0.0200$ A. [M1 A1]
(b) $V_2=IR_2=4.00$ V. [M1 A1]
(c) Parallel connection gives a smaller total resistance than either branch, so for the same supply voltage the total current is larger. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt:
A 40 Ω resistor and a 0.050 S conductor are combined.
(i) Calculate their total resistance in series. (1)
(ii) Calculate their total conductance in parallel. (1)

(i) Show that the p.d. across 4.7 kΩ in series with 2.2 kΩ across 6.0 V is about 4.1 V. (1)
(ii) An analogue voltmeter across the 4.7 kΩ reads 3.0 V. Show its resistance is about 4 kΩ. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) 6.0 × 4.7/6.9 = 4.1 V [B1]
(ii) 3.0 V means parallel combination equals 2.2 kΩ [M1]
1/Rv = 1/2200 − 1/4700 [M1]
Rv = 4.1 kΩ [A1]

questions.prompt: A potato cell reads 0.90 V on a 1 MΩ voltmeter and 0.45 V on a 4.1 kΩ voltmeter. Estimate its internal resistance and state an assumption. (3)
questions.solution:
emf ≈ 0.90 V [M1]
Half the emf is lost, so r ≈ 4.1 kΩ [A1]
Assumes the 1 MΩ meter draws negligible current [B1]

questions.prompt:
A 300 Ω strain gauge is in series with a 500 Ω resistor across 6.00 V.
(i) Calculate the p.d. across the resistor. (2)
(ii) Under tension, this p.d. drops to 3.70 V. Calculate the new gauge resistance. (2)

A solar cell's maximum (short-circuit) current is 70 mA.
(i) Calculate the maximum number of electrons per second. (2)
(ii) Suggest why there is a maximum. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) 0.070 ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ [M1]
= 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s⁻¹ [A1]
(ii) Limited by the number of photons absorbed per second [B1]

questions.prompt:
A wire of conductivity 2.0 × 10⁶ S m⁻¹ and area 0.20 mm² has 2.0 V across 0.40 m.
(i) Calculate the current. (2)
(ii) Estimate the drift velocity (n ≈ 10²⁸ m⁻³). (2)
A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω delivers 1.0 A. Calculate the power wasted inside the cell. (2)
Resistors R and 4R are in series across a supply. Find the ratio of the power in 4R to the power in R. (2)

A 12 V solar panel (internal resistance 10 Ω) charges a 9.0 V battery (internal resistance 3.0 Ω) through a 4.7 Ω resistor.
(i) Calculate the initial charging current. (2)
(ii) A 400 mA h battery charges at a mean 0.10 A. Estimate the time. (2)

A copper wire 1.5 m long, radius 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m, has resistance 0.13 Ω.
(i) Calculate its conductivity. (3)
(ii) Calculate the drift velocity for 2.3 A (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³). (2)
Explain how increasing temperature affects the conductivity of metals and semiconductors. (4)
questions.solution:
Metals: number of free electrons barely changes [B1]
Increased lattice vibrations reduce conductivity [B1]
Semiconductors: many more charge carriers released (σ = Ce^(−E/kT)) [B1]
Conductivity increases greatly [B1]

questions.prompt: A 12.0 V motor's stall current is 3.0 A. Calculate the coil resistance. (2)
questions.solution:
At stall there is no back emf [M1]
R = 4.0 Ω [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A lamp has 4.0 V across it at 2.5 A. Show R = 1.6 Ω. (1)
(ii) Its conductivity is 1.8 × 10⁷ S m⁻¹ when R = 0.93 Ω. Calculate its conductivity at 2.5 A. (2)
Explain why filament conductivity falls as current increases. (2)
questions.solution:
Temperature rises [B1]
Ions vibrate more, so electrons collide more often [B1]

questions.prompt: A cell with internal resistance 1.0 Ω drives 2.0 A through a 3.0 Ω resistor. Calculate the e.m.f. (2)
Wire X has 3.0 Ω. Wire Y has half the resistivity, half the length and a quarter of the area. Find Y's resistance. (2)
An LDR of 7.0 kΩ is in series with 10.0 kΩ on 6.0 V. Calculate the p.d. across the LDR. (2)
Identical resistors are added in parallel across an ideal cell. How does total power vary with their number? (2)
questions.solution:
Each dissipates V²/R [M1]
Total power ∝ N (straight line through origin) [A1]

questions.prompt: Define the sensitivity of a sensor and give its unit for an LDR measured in lux. (2)
questions.solution:
Change in output ÷ change in input [B1]
Ω lx⁻¹ [B1]

questions.prompt: A 0.50 m wire with area 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² has resistance 4.0 Ω. Calculate its conductivity. (2)
Two identical cells (ε, r) are connected in series. State the intercept and gradient of their V–I graph. (2)
A 9.0 V supply drives current through 2.0 Ω and 4.0 Ω in series. Calculate the current and p.d. across each. (2)
Heaters X (12 V) and Y (6 V) give equal power. Find R_X/R_Y, and d_X/d_Y if made from equal lengths of the same wire. (2)
Show a 30 kA lightning strike lasting 250 μs carries less than 8 C. (2)

A 230 V, 46 A shower heats water from 22 °C to 39 °C.
(i) Calculate the energy for 1 kg. (2)
(ii) Calculate the time for this. (2)
A 1.5 V cell drives a 30 Ω resistor (0.4 V across it) in series with R₂. Calculate R₂. (2)
A nichrome wire (diameter 5.6 × 10⁻⁴ m) carries 0.30 A, and p.d. rises 1.3 V per metre. Calculate its conductivity. (3)
questions.solution:
A = 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ m² [M1]
R per metre = 4.3 Ω m⁻¹ [M1]
σ = 9 × 10⁵ S m⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: A 12 V divider of two 200 Ω resistors gives 6.0 V. A 200 Ω load is connected across one resistor. Find V_out. (2)
Give the e.m.f. and internal resistance of two identical cells (ε, r) in series. (1)

Electromagnetic radiation has frequency $5\times10^{14}$ Hz.
(a) Calculate its wavelength in vacuum. (2)
(b) Calculate the energy of one photon using $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s. (2)
(c) Explain what is meant by diffraction and state when it is most noticeable. (3)
questions.solution:
(a) $\lambda=c/f=6.000\times10^{-7}$ m. [M1 A1]
(b) $E=hf=3.315\times10^{-19}$ J. [M1 A1]
(c) Diffraction is spreading of waves at an aperture/edge and is greatest when the aperture size is comparable with the wavelength. [B1 B1 B1]

questions.prompt:
An electron is accelerated through 5.0 kV.
(i) Calculate its speed (non-relativistic). (2)
(ii) Justify ignoring relativity. (1)
(iii) Calculate its de Broglie wavelength. (2)
Explain how electron diffraction rings show both wave-like and particle-like behaviour, using phasors. (4)
questions.solution:
Each electron is detected at a single point – particle-like [B1]
The pattern of rings builds up – wave-like [B1]
Phasors for all paths through the graphite are added [B1]
Bright where phasors line up; probability ∝ (resultant amplitude)² [B1]

questions.prompt: Light at 30° in air passes through glass (2.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) into water (2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Calculate the refraction angle in water. (3)
Electrons have momentum 1.2 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹ and pass through slits 1.0 μm apart. Calculate the wavelength and angle to the first maximum. (3)
Single electrons pass through two slits one at a time and a pattern slowly builds up. Explain what this shows. (2)
questions.solution:
Each electron arrives at a point – particle [B1]
Fringes build up – each electron behaves as a wave through both slits [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a bright line forms in a particular direction from a multi-slit grating. (2)
questions.solution:
Waves from adjacent slits have path difference nλ in that direction [B1]
Arrive in phase and superpose constructively [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain where an object must be placed to form a magnified real image with a converging lens. (2)
questions.solution:
Between f and 2f from the lens [B1]
Image forms beyond 2f, magnified and inverted [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how phasors give the intensity at a point in a double-slit pattern. (2)
questions.solution:
Phasors from each slit are added tip-to-tail [B1]
Intensity ∝ square of the resultant amplitude [B1]

questions.prompt:
A lens projects an image onto a wall 2.0 m away from a display 0.025 m from the lens.
(i) Calculate the lens power. (3)
(ii) State the magnification. (1)

An electron is confined in a box of width 0.10 nm with Eₙ = n²h²/8md².
(i) Explain why the model gives discrete energy levels. (2)
(ii) Calculate the frequency of the photon emitted in the n = 3 to n = 1 transition. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Electron forms standing waves that must fit the box (d = nλ/2) [B1]
Only certain wavelengths, so only certain momenta and energies [B1]
(ii) E₁ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)² ÷ (8 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁻²⁰) = 6.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ J [M1]
ΔE = 8E₁ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁷ J [M1]
f = 7.3 × 10¹⁶ Hz [A1]

questions.prompt: A graph of fringe spacing against slit-screen distance has gradient 1.2 × 10⁻³ ± 5%. Slit separation is (0.50 ± 0.10) mm. Calculate the wavelength and its percentage uncertainty. (4)
Describe how the intensity through two polarisers changes as one is rotated through 360°. (2)
questions.solution:
Maximum when axes are parallel, zero when perpendicular [B1]
Two maxima and two minima per rotation [B1]

questions.prompt:
Rubidium's threshold frequency is 5.1 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
(i) Calculate its work function. (2)
(ii) Explain why Einstein's equation gives the maximum kinetic energy. (1)

A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities.
(a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2)
(b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2)
(c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution:
(a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. [M1 A1]
(b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. [B1 B1]
(c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt: Microwave intensity through a rotated grille is predicted to be ∝ cos²θ. Describe how to test this with data and state how you'd conclude. (3)
questions.solution:
Plot detector reading against cos²θ [B1]
Straight line through origin supports the model [B1]
Check points lie within error bars [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to use a dot plot of repeated tube-area measurements to find the mean and percentage uncertainty. (3)
questions.solution:
Identify and exclude outliers [B1]
Calculate the mean of the remaining values [B1]
Uncertainty = half the spread; % = uncertainty ÷ mean × 100 [B1]

questions.prompt: A graph of ln(count rate) against t has gradient −0.0050 s⁻¹. Calculate the decay constant and half-life. (3)
Explain why counting in 10 s intervals over several minutes is suitable for protactinium (half-life about 70 s). (2)
questions.solution:
Gives several readings per half-life [B1]
Each count large enough to limit random variation [B1]

questions.prompt: A worst-fit line of pressure against temperature has gradient 0.36 kPa K⁻¹ and passes through (300 K, 101 kPa). Calculate the temperature where pressure would be zero. (4)
questions.solution:
p = 0.36T + c; c = 101 − 108 = −7 kPa [M1]
0 = 0.36T − 7 [M1]
T = 19 K [A1]
Compare with 0 K to judge uncertainty [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what a systematic error is and how part of a flask being above the water bath could cause one. (3)
questions.solution:
Systematic error shifts all readings the same way [B1]
Gas in the exposed part is cooler than the bath [B1]
Measured pressures too low at high temperatures [B1]

questions.prompt: Estimate the uncertainty in measuring a gas column height with a metre rule and justify it. (2)
questions.solution:
About ±2 mm [B1]
Reading both ends to ±1 mm; meniscus and parallax [B1]

questions.prompt:

questions.prompt: Describe how to record the p.d. across a capacitor as it discharges through 4.7 kΩ. (4)

Charge the capacitor from the supply with a switch, then switch to discharge through the resistor [B1]
Voltmeter across the capacitor [B1]
Record V every 10 s with a stopwatch [B1]
Repeat and average / use a data logger [B1]

Gradient uncertainty 0.60 × 10⁻⁷ V m (6.7%) [M1]
h = (4.7 ± 0.3) × 10⁻³⁴ J s [A1]

questions.solution:
Beam area increases by a factor of 4 [M1]
Same power spread over 4 times the area, so L/4 [A1]

Developing new technology / materials [B1]
